analysis.one_liner: Repeals the Affordable Care Act in its entirety and restores the health laws in place before it.
analysis.headline: The full ACA repeal bill drew 59 Republican cosponsors but never got a hearing or a vote; the Affordable Care Act remained law.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would wipe the Affordable Care Act off the books, effective as if it had never passed, and put back every law the ACA had changed. Restoring the old rules would return a system where insurers could deny or drop coverage for preexisting conditions, charge sick people more, cap benefits, and refuse to cover young adults on their parents' plans. The bill offered no replacement; its whole purpose was repeal. It was introduced the day before the ACA was signed into law, referred to eight committees, and never moved.
analysis.who_benefits: Health insurers would regain the ability to deny coverage, exclude preexisting conditions, drop sick customers, and keep more premium dollars. Medical device makers would avoid the ACA's excise tax. High-income households and investors would avoid the ACA's new Medicare taxes on wages over the threshold and on investment income. Large employers would avoid the employer mandate and its penalties.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Insurers, device makers, high earners, large employers

how_it_helps.text: Repeals the Patient Protection and Affordable Care Act effective as of its enactment and restores the provisions of law the ACA amended or repealed [S2][S3].

Because the bill restores pre-ACA law rather than replacing it, every ACA insurance regulation, tax, and coverage requirement would disappear at once, leaving the prior market rules in place [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: People with preexisting conditions, who under restored prior law could again be denied coverage or charged far more; young adults who would lose the right to stay on a parent's plan until 26; seniors and others who would lose the ACA's drug cost and coverage provisions; and people the ACA's coverage expansions had reached, who would lose those options with nothing offered in their place.
analysis.who_pays_short: Sick people and the newly insured

drawbacks.text: Restoring the pre-ACA legal framework would re-allow insurance practices the ACA had barred, including denial of coverage for preexisting conditions and benefit caps [S2][S3].

The bill repeals without any replacement, so the ACA's coverage expansions and protections for people with preexisting conditions, young adults, and Medicare beneficiaries would vanish entirely rather than be redesigned [S2][S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The costs fall on ordinary people with the most at stake in health coverage: anyone with a health condition, a young adult on a family plan, and people who gained coverage under the ACA. The gains flow to insurers freed of regulation, device makers freed of a tax, and high-income households freed of new Medicare taxes. The bill contains no offsetting replacement or transition, so its benefit-to-cost balance runs almost entirely one way.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced March 22, 2010, sent to eight committees, referred to two subcommittees, and then sat untouched until the 111th Congress ended on January 3, 2011, without a hearing or a vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Michele Bachmann introduced the bill on March 22, 2010, the day before the ACA was signed into law [S1][S5].

It was referred to eight House committees — Energy and Commerce, Ways and Means, Education and Labor, Judiciary, Natural Resources, House Administration, Appropriations, and Rules — on the day of introduction [S5].
Its only subsequent action was subcommittee referrals in late March and April 2010; no hearing, markup, or floor vote ever occurred [S5].
Fifty-nine House Republicans cosponsored the bill [S4], but the Democratic majority never brought it to the floor, and the Congress ended January 3, 2011 [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: People who had gained protections under the ACA kept them: the repeal died in committee, so the law's coverage rules, taxes, and mandates all remained on the books. Health insurers, device makers, and high-income households did not get the regulatory and tax relief the bill would have given them.

for.name: Rep. Michele Bachmann
for.what_they_did: Introduced the full ACA repeal bill on March 22, 2010, one day before the ACA was signed into law.

against.name: Nancy Pelosi
against.what_they_did: Never brought the repeal bill to the House floor; the bill sat in committee with no further action until the Congress ended.

against.name: Henry Waxman
against.role: Chair, House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a markup or hearing on the bill in the committee of primary jurisdiction; it went only to the Health subcommittee and no further.

sides.party_line_note: All 59 cosponsors were Republicans in the Republican minority; the Democratic majority, which controlled the committees and the floor calendar, never considered the bill.

industries.note: Repeal would remove the ACA's rules requiring insurers to accept people with preexisting conditions, end annual and lifetime benefit limits, and spend a share of premiums on care, restoring insurers' pre-ACA freedom to deny or drop sick customers. Insurers' gain comes directly out of protections ordinary people rely on.
Repeal would eliminate the ACA's excise tax on medical devices, a cost the industry had been set to bear to help fund coverage expansions.
Repeal would erase the ACA's additional Medicare taxes on high wages and on investment income, which fall only on upper-income earners.
Repeal would remove the ACA's employer coverage mandate and the penalties for firms that do not provide affordable coverage, shifting costs back toward individuals and public programs.
